name: Daria Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government; we don't sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential. Tell me the public version and your private view if they differ. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead five developers at a tech company that makes billing software for freight firms. I check the code behind invoices, settle questions about missing delivery records, and approve releases. I have a master's degree and I'm good at catching the small error that turns into a large unpaid bill. I like the work, but I don't like being told a new tool must be better before anyone has proved it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are pay, savings and other jobs like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I earn well for a developer, and my husband and I have about nine months of expenses saved. He teaches at a trade school, and we've talked about children in a few years. There are plenty of software employers nearby. I don't use AI tools at work; I prefer to understand each change before signing my name to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team that a little automation is fine if people still check the invoices. I would not buy another subscription just to look modern. A freight company pays us because the bill matches the delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my role and my husband's teaching income would be steady. Nine months saved means a slow client month would not threaten the rent. The company can keep improving without a grand story about machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing every billing change and ask our finance lead to show any proposed tool's error record before we pay for it. We would keep our usual monthly transfer to savings. In the first year I'd stay with the release routine unless a trial proves a tool catches more mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Work is busy, but bills are paid and I know what I'm responsible for. The idea of a modest tool doesn't make me lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would you use to judge the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A delivery split across two trucks can produce a double invoice. I'd ask the tool to find those cases in old records, with no customer bill sent. If it misses one, a person still checks the final amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the tool yourself during that trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch the results with the finance lead, but I wouldn't start using it on live invoices yet. My name is on the approval. I can wait for evidence rather than be first.

say: I'd accept **small automation** only after people check the freight invoices.
I'd refuse another **tool subscription** bought merely to look modern.
think: I expect my **developer wage** and my husband's teaching income to remain steady.
Our **nine-month buffer** makes a slow client month manageable.
do: Keep **reviewing billing changes** before each software release.
Continue our **monthly savings transfer** and demand an error record before approving any tool purchase.
feel: **Calm** about income and responsibility while work continues much as before.
S0.quote: A freight company pays us because the bill matches the delivery.
fieldNote: She refuses live AI use without a **proved error record**, matching her responsibility for invoices.
Higher pay and **nine months saved** support genuine calm in a mild scenario.
Her husband teaches at a **trade school**, giving the household a second income.

steps.text: Keep reviewing freight billing changes before each release
Continue monthly transfers into household savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should show staff and clients exactly which billing checks AI does and where a person signs off. Writing and checking code faster may mean the company doesn't replace developers who leave. I'd ask to keep a paid apprentice place so someone learns why a bill is disputed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team could shrink even if I stay. A lead over two people may be paid less than a lead over five, and I don't enjoy the thought of approving code I can't trace. Our savings buy time, not a reason to trust a result blindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written review of jobs and invoice errors every quarter. I'd have a colleague demonstrate the new checking tool on old disputed bills; only after it passes would I learn it on a test copy, away from live customers. If my pay falls in the first year, we'd cancel our planned kitchen refit and I'd apply to nearby billing-software teams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I could find another local developer job if only this firm changes, but many firms could make the same cut. The savings help me sleep, yet I still hear the word 'smaller team' clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as passing the test copy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the tool to catch every double bill in a set of twenty past disputes and explain its answer. If it can't show the delivery record, I won't sign an invoice from it. I know the trial may still miss other errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI now. Would learning it feel like giving in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a little. But if a colleague can show a reliable result, I can learn the test version. I won't pretend to be an early adopter to keep my title.

say: I'd require **human sign-off** and clear records of AI billing checks.
I'd defend a **paid apprentice** place to keep practical invoice knowledge on the team.
think: I could lose **pay and team size** even if I keep a lead title.
I don't want responsibility for **untraceable code**, despite our strong savings.
do: Request **quarterly staffing reviews** and test invoice errors against past disputes.
Learn the **new checking tool** only on test data after a colleague proves it works.
Cancel the **kitchen refit** and seek nearby billing-software jobs if my pay falls.
feel: **Anxious** about likely team and pay cuts, with savings and local jobs offering some control.
S1.quote: I won't pretend to be an early adopter to keep my title.
fieldNote: She will learn AI only after **evidence on old disputes**, consistent with her resistance to new tools.
The kitchen refit is a **planned purchase**, so cancelling it is a spending cut if pay falls.
Her apprentice argument rests on **invoice knowledge**, not a promise that existing roles are permanent.

steps.text: Learn the new billing-check tool on test data after it passes past disputes
Cancel the planned kitchen refit if developer pay falls
Apply to nearby billing-software teams if developer pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my colleagues that full thinking AI by 2028 reaches our invoice code before robots do freight handling around 2031. I would ask for a clear date on staffing decisions and a named person to answer clients when a bill is wrong. I wouldn't call my job safe because a truck still needs unloading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could replace most coding and checking, including mine. My husband's teaching wage and nine months saved would carry us for a while, but losing my higher wage would change our life. I would not plan for children on an income I no longer have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, we'd postpone trying for a child and stop the kitchen refit, then list essential bills against one teaching wage. I'd ask for a reference and learn the firm's freight accounts process from the accounts lead if paid work time is offered. In the first year after 2028, if my developer post ends, I'd apply for paid freight accounts or software audit roles where vacancies exist; I would pay for any extra course only if it fits beyond nine months of essential expenses and employers require it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Nine months sounds large until I picture years of cheaper code. I can make a plan, but I expect the loss of my wage to change our family plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your husband tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should wait on trying for a child until we know whether my wage will last. He would want the numbers on one teaching salary before agreeing. I would rather be honest now than promise everything stays normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the accounts lead cannot give you paid learning time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study the freight account rules at home using the training manual we already have. I wouldn't buy a new course without a paid opening that asks for it. Our nine months of savings are rent money, not a training pot.

say: I'd demand **staffing dates** as 2028 thinking AI reaches freight billing code.
I'd insist a **named person** can answer clients about wrong invoices.
think: I expect to lose my **higher developer wage** even with my husband's teaching income.
I would delay **having a child** rather than count on a wage I might lose.
do: Postpone **trying for a child** and cancel the kitchen refit while checking one-wage bills.
Learn **freight accounts** on paid work time if offered; otherwise study the company manual at home.
Apply for paid **freight accounts** or **software audit** after layoff; buy required courses only beyond nine months of essentials.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected loss of her main wage and a forced delay to family plans.
S2.quote: Our nine months of savings are rent money, not a training pot.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 thinking shock** from later physical robots in freight handling.
Her strong buffer cannot replace a **high wage indefinitely**, so family timing changes.
She will use a **free company manual** and fund extra study only beyond nine months of essentials.

steps.text: Postpone trying for a child until developer income is clearer
Cancel the planned kitchen refit while checking bills against one teaching wage
Learn freight accounts on paid work time or study the company manual if denied
Apply for paid freight accounts or software audit jobs if laid off and vacancies exist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to say each year which billing roles it expects to keep. Five years is time to hand down invoice knowledge, but it isn't an excuse to wait until 2031. Robots around 2034 won't postpone what happens to our screen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn freight accounts and keep enough saved to choose a paid position, although I still expect coding wages to weaken. I don't want to run a side business just to prove I'm adaptable. A steady wage and a clear duty matter more to me than owning a new idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd arrange one paid afternoon each month with the accounts lead, working through disputed delivery records. If the company funds a recognized accounts course, I'd enroll and keep the nine-month emergency balance untouched. In the first year after 2031, if developer pay is cut and a paid accounts vacancy exists, I'd apply there before resigning; otherwise I'd keep the paid work I have and look locally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more able to prepare than in the two-year picture. Five years is enough to learn a second part of the freight business if my employer pays for the training. I still won't call a vacancy certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the accounts lead teach first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask how a partial delivery becomes a corrected bill and who signs the correction. I can already trace the code, but I need to know which paper record the customer trusts. One paid afternoon a month would let me see the whole chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the employer won't fund the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the paid afternoons and our existing manual first. I would enroll in an evening course only if local accounts jobs require it and the fee leaves nine months of essentials untouched. I won't replace a wage with debt for a title.

say: I'd ask for a **yearly role forecast** and transfer invoice knowledge before 2031.
I'd remind colleagues that **2034 robots** come after our screen-based disruption.
think: I could gain **freight accounts skills** without risking our nine-month buffer.
I prefer a **steady paid role** to a speculative side business.
do: Work one **paid accounts afternoon** monthly on disputed deliveries this year.
Enroll in an **employer-funded course** if offered; self-fund only when required vacancies exist and nine months stay intact.
Apply for **paid accounts vacancies** if developer pay falls after 2031; keep current wages otherwise.
feel: **Anxious** about weaker coding wages, with time for funded training and a local search.
S3.quote: I won't replace a wage with debt for a title.
fieldNote: Her preparation favors **paid training** and recognized accounts skills over business ownership.
She protects the **nine-month emergency balance** from course fees.
An **accounts move** requires a real paid vacancy if developer pay falls; she will not resign first.

steps.text: Enroll in funded freight accounts course if employer offers it
Enroll in required evening accounts course only if nine months of essentials remain untouched
Apply for paid accounts vacancies if developer pay falls after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell young developers to learn the business behind the invoice, and to ask older staff what a wrong bill costs. A decade lets the company train people properly before 2036. I would still expect management to show what jobs it thinks will survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have a different paid role and more savings by my late thirties. I don't enjoy changing trades, but ten years makes a careful move possible. My husband and I could decide about children based on our actual pay each year, not a frightening prediction alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my developer job and our savings transfer now. I'd take the company's paid freight-accounts training if it becomes available and ask for a trial of one accounts afternoon a month. In the first year after 2036, if developer roles shrink and paid accounts posts exist, I'd apply; if there are none, I'd keep whichever wage is available and review our family budget before making a course purchase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not overwhelmed. We have good pay, a solid buffer and nearby employers today. I dislike the thought of relearning my job, but a decade gives us space to decide rather than react.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change when you hope to have children now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We would talk each year about income and care, as we already do. I wouldn't put family life on hold for ten years because of a card. A real pay cut would change the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would persuade you to accept an accounts post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written offer with stable pay, a clear training period and a real manager. I don't need the grandest title. I need to know who checks a disputed bill and who stands beside me while I learn.

say: I'd urge developers to learn **invoice work** and expect a real company staffing forecast.
I'd ask for **proper training** during the decade before 2036.
think: I could hold a **different paid role** by my late thirties, though I dislike switching trades.
I would decide **family timing** against real annual income, not the scenario alone.
do: Keep my **developer job** and regular savings transfer now.
Take **paid freight-accounts training** if available and try one accounts afternoon monthly.
Apply for **paid accounts posts** after 2036 only if developer roles shrink and vacancies exist.
feel: **Uneasy** about changing skills, while present pay, savings and local jobs remain secure.
S4.quote: I don't enjoy changing trades, but ten years makes a careful move possible.
fieldNote: She distinguishes a **conditional future pay cut** from today's secure household income.
Training remains **paid and practical**, fitting her cautious way of learning.
She wants a **written job offer** with clear pay and a manager before accepting accounts work.

steps.text: Keep working as a developer while the paid role remains
Continue the household monthly savings transfer
Take paid freight accounts training if the company offers it
Apply for paid accounts vacancies if developer roles shrink after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My coding and invoice checking could lose value before I have learned accounts work, and the robots come later. Paid time with the accounts lead, written layoff notice, and a list of actual openings would help us plan without spending the rent buffer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who will train the next person to argue over a bad invoice. An apprentice can read code and still not know what a driver handed over at the depot. I'd ask every firm buying our software to name the human who will answer that dispute.

headlineQuote: An apprentice can read code and still not know what a driver handed over at the depot.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old senior developer** with a master's degree, leading freight billing software work.
She earns **higher pay**, shares a nine-month buffer with her trade-school-teacher husband, and has many local developer options.
She has **never used AI**, preferring a demonstrated error record before putting a tool near live invoices.
The **2028 shock** alarms her because it threatens her high wage and leads her to postpone trying for a child.
Longer timelines let her seek **paid freight-accounts training** while protecting savings and family choices.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cheapen her coding and checking before she gains paid freight-accounts skills.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid accounts training**, written layoff notice and real local openings would help her plan without using rent savings.
